content: The studies included in the analysis comprised three retrospective studies and one combined prospective/retrospective study. A small percentage (3%) of the studies utilized whole blood samples drawn from veins, while another 3% used frozen samples. Approximately 7% of the studies were conducted in the United States, and 7% were conducted in lowand middle-income countries. In the meta-analysis evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the Xpert HBV DNA viral load assay, six studies involving 1,577 samples collected across seven countries between 2017 and 2019 were included. When compared to a laboratory-based reference standard, the pooled sensitivity and specificity of the Xpert HBV DNA viral load assay were 96% (95% CI: 94–98%) and 98% (95% CI: 90–100%), respectively. For other point-of-care (POC) assays, such as the HBV-LAMP Assay, Duplex real-time RAA, HBV-MCDA-LFB Assay, and Cas12a-DETECTR Assay, nine studies with a total of 1,513 samples collected across five countries between 2015 and 2022 were included. Approximately 2% of the samples originated from India and Vietnam in South-East Asia, and 6% of the studies were conducted in middle-income countries. The pooled sensitivity and specificity for these POC assays were also high, at approximately 98% (95% CI: 94–99%) and 99% (95% CI: 93–100%), respectively. The quality of the included studies was assessed using QUADAS-2-adapted methodologies. Variations in patient selection methods across studies may have introduced bias in sensitivity and specificity estimates. The influence of reference tests on bias was deemed unclear or low, while the index tests exhibited a higher degree of bias. The risk associated with flow and timing was rated as low or unclear. The overall quality of evidence was graded using the GRADE framework. Despite all included studies being observational, the overall quality of evidence was not downgraded. However, several studies were funded by diagnostic companies, which may have influenced the results, particularly in terms of small sample effects and publication bias. The overall certainty for both sensitivity and specificity was determined to be moderate to high. The findings indicate that HBV POC DNA viral load assays demonstrate excellent diagnostic performance, making them a reliable and convenient alternative to conventional laboratory-based assays for quantifying HBV DNA in clinical practice. These assays can guide clinical decision-making regarding antiviral therapy across diverse healthcare settings. Centralized laboratory systems for HBV DNA testing often require robust sample transport and result return systems, with turnaround times ranging from days to weeks. These systems typically utilize large, automated machines, such as the Abbott m2000, Hologic Panther, and Roche 6800/8800 Systems, which offer high throughput at lower costs. However, they necessitate a cold chain for transporting serum or plasma samples. Near point-of-care (POC) platforms provide an opportunity for on-site testing at facilities where patients receive care, such as district hospitals or high-volume health centers. These platforms are smaller and can be placed in controlled environments, requiring trained laboratory or healthcare staff to perform the tests. Current assays require serum, plasma, or venous blood specimens, with assay run times typically ranging from 1–2 hours and result turnaround times from hours to days. The hub-and-spoke model for testing allows on-site testing at a central hub site, with samples transported from nearby spoke sites. This model can reduce turnaround times and sample transport needs compared to centralized testing. Molecular testing platforms can be distributed across multiple hubs within a district or province, each serving a network of surrounding health facilities. The market for quality-assured HBV DNA POC products is limited, with only two manufacturers offering such products for near POC platforms. WHO has recently extended its prequalification process to include quantitative HBV DNA assays, encouraging manufacturers to submit applications. This process typically takes over a year. As suppliers achieve WHO prequalification status, it will enable the prioritization of quality, accessible HBV DNA products and facilitate their expansion into high-burden countries. Global procurement volumes for HBV DNA testing remain far below expected needs, with at least 400,000 tests procured for lowand middle-income countries in 2021. While procurement volumes increased by 70% from 2016 to 2019, growth declined in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Sales volumes are expected to grow moving forward, with most sales attributed to Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and smaller sales in Latin America. The introduction of Global Access Program pricing ensures that HBV DNA assays are available at standardized base prices for select lowand middle-income countries. However, significant gaps in equitable pricing persist, as additional costs such as distributor fees, supply chain costs, and machine servicing can increase the total cost by up to 30%. For hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) testing, updated WHO guidelines recommend its use in pregnant women who screen positive for HBsAg to determine eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis with tenofovir, particularly where antenatal HBV DNA testing is unavailable. However, limited national policies and implementation of HBeAg algorithms, as well as concerns about test performance, have hindered widespread adoption. If countries validate HBeAg testing, it may provide an opportunity for broader adoption to enable prophylaxis determination, especially in settings with limited access to HBV viral load testing. The market for HBeAg products includes both rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and laboratory-based immunoassays, but options with stringent regulatory approvals are limited. Addressing these gaps in access and pricing will be critical to improving the availability and adoption of HBV diagnostic tools globally.
